title: Expressions with do and make
subtitle: do the housework, make a profit, do away with, make up for
summary: Use the phrasal verbs and collocations built on do and make, and know which of the two verbs each expression takes.

lesson.heading: Phrasal verbs with do and make
rows: move in the direction of; lead to
think about, have an opinion of

lesson.heading: The phrasal verbs in use
lesson.text: Notice that **make of** is almost always used in a question (*What do you make of ... ?*), and that **make off** often comes with **with** when someone leaves taking something that is not theirs.

examples.text: We'll have to **do without** a holiday this year as money is so short.
It should be our ambition to **do away with** poverty in the world.
Let's **make for** the city centre and look for a restaurant there.
What do you **make of** the new software?
examples.note: = what is your opinion of it?

examples.text: He **made off** as soon as he heard their car turn into the drive.
The superb food at the hotel **made up for** the uncomfortable rooms.

lesson.heading: One phrasal verb, several meanings
rows: fasten; renovate; tie into a bundle or wrap
claim or pretend; manage to see; understand
compose or invent; constitute or form; put cosmetics on; prepare by mixing ingredients; make something more numerous or complete
lesson.note: With the meaning 'understand', make out is normally used with can or could and a negative: I can't make him out.

lesson.heading: Those meanings in sentences
lesson.text: The context tells you which meaning is intended. Compare these examples of the same three phrasal verbs.

examples.text: Your shoelaces are untied. **Do** them **up** or you'll trip over.
We're planning to **do up** our bathroom at the weekend.
Can you **make out** the little white house on the mountain side?
He **made out** that he had never loved anyone else.
examples.note: = claimed, and it may well not be true

examples.text: A human being is **made up of** many, often conflicting, desires.
Take this prescription to the chemist and she'll **make** it **up** for you.

left.label: do = activity, work, duty
left.text: Use **do** for jobs and activities, especially ones that repeat.
examples: I have to **do my homework** before I go out.
Her company **does a lot of business** in East Asia.
I go to the gym, so I **do** plenty of **exercise**.
It doesn't matter if you pass, as long as you **do your best**.

right.label: make = an end product
right.text: Use **make** when something new comes out of it: tea, a cake, a noise, a decision, a profit.
examples: Shall I **make a cup of tea**?
Companies that once **made a huge profit** are now going bankrupt.
We need to **make a decision** today.
I try not to **make too many mistakes**.
Dressing smartly helps you to **make a good impression**.

lesson.heading: More collocations to learn as whole phrases
lesson.note: Make allowances for someone = consider their situation and not judge them harshly. Make a fuss of someone = give them a lot of attention and treat them well.

lesson.text: Remember the sentence that contains both: *When I do my homework, I try not to make too many mistakes.* Not ~~make my homework~~ or ~~do mistakes~~.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrasal verb with its meaning.
Does each expression take do or make?
Can you make out the little white house on the mountain side? Here make out means ...
exercises.explanation: With can/could, make out often means manage to see something that is hard to see.

exercises.prompt: A human being is made up of many, often conflicting, desires. Here made up of means ...
exercises.explanation: Make up = constitute or form; with this meaning it is usually passive: X is made up of Y.

exercises.prompt: He made out that he had never loved anyone else. She believed him. Here made out means ...
exercises.explanation: Make out = claim, and it implies that what is claimed may well not be true.

exercises.prompt: The present was beautifully done ___ in gold paper.
exercises.explanation: Do up here means tie or wrap into a bundle or parcel.

exercises.prompt: We agreed that we could do ___ the old fireplace in the corner.
exercises.explanation: Do away with = abolish, get rid of.

exercises.prompt: At first we could not make ___ what the photographs were, but we wiped them clean.
exercises.explanation: Can't make something out = can't manage to see or understand it.

exercises.prompt: We spent an enjoyable evening making ___ stories to explain why the pictures had been hidden.
exercises.explanation: Make up a story = invent it.

exercises.statement: Vast amounts of money do not always make of happiness.
exercises.explanation: Vast amounts of money do not always make for happiness. Make for = lead to.

exercises.statement: Thieves robbed the bank and made off with £1,000,000.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Make off with something = leave hurriedly taking it.

exercises.prompt: You must make ___ the fact that he's only seven years old.
exercises.explanation: Make allowances for = consider someone's situation and not judge them harshly.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to make a famous 1960s slogan.
exercises.explanation: Both love and war go with make, never with do.
